Hidden ingredients

 

Once upon a time, investors had to hire a human mutual-fund manager to bet their savings on niche categories that sounded promising. But those pros have a tendency to stray from their benchmarks—often in the wrong direction.

 

With around 2,000 index ETFs now available at the click of a button, Americans can buy and sell the exact baskets of stocks those fund managers use as a target. It seems like that leaves nothing to chance. Stay humble if that works out, though—it can be because of some surprise ingredients.

 

Consider a weird turn of events in early 2021. Value investors were eating the market’s dust and small-capitalization value stocks had been doing particularly poorly. Investors who gritted their teeth and bought funds tracking a leading small cap value index made impressive gains, but not because they had identified some market turning point. They were about a year early.

 

Instead, that was when meme-stock mania briefly gripped the market. Two money losing companies, GameStop and AMC Entertainment, temporarily found themselves as the largest constituents of the usually dowdy Russell 2000 Value Index. That benchmark beat the S&P 500 by a mile during the first quarter.

 
 
 
 

Three years later, the entire Russell 2000 index got a lucky break. Red hot Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) and Super Micro Computer got so big so quickly that they didn’t remotely qualify as small-cap stocks.

 

Back then, though, the Russell’s owner only reconstituted the index once a year, in late June. Those two stocks accounted for one-third of the index’s gain in the first quarter of 2024. Then both were booted from the index around the time they stalled.

 
 
 
 

And investors this spring who thought they were buying themselves a bit of diversification from AI-mania by hitching their wagons to developing economies got an extra dose of what was going gangbusters.

 

Some wealthy countries with cutting-edge tech companies remain in MSCI’s Emerging Markets Index because they haven’t made market reforms that the index provider would like to see. They dominate its benchmark now. 

 

Taiwan alone, with a population of 23 million, carries more weight than poorer, more populous Turkey, Mexico, Brazil, India and South Africa combined. South Korea is a close second in the index.

 

In May, just three chip makers, Taiwan’s TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, accounted for more of the index’s gain than its 1,100 or so other stocks.

 

It feels great to act on a hunch and profit, but that ETF you bought might not have gone up because of what’s on the label. Luck plays a bigger role in short-term index moves than we realize.

 

Go ahead and buy cheap index ETFs to diversify, but keep your day job.
